h1: Oak chips and spirals for barrel character without a barrel
title: Oak Chips and Spirals in Homebrew | Craft Beer School
desc: How to add barrel character to homebrew with oak chips, cubes and spirals: oak types, toast levels, amounts, contact times and sanitising.
teaser: No barrel, no problem. A handful of toasted oak and some patience gives a stout or barleywine real wood character.
standfirst: Barrels are expensive, leak and need constant care. Oak alternatives give homebrewers most of the flavour for very little money. Here is how to choose the oak, how much to use and how long to leave it.
sections:
Oak gives vanilla, coconut, toast, caramel, spice and a dry tannic grip. Toasting the wood breaks down its structure into these flavour compounds. In a barrel, beer also picks up character from whatever the barrel held before, such as whisky or wine. It also changes with slow oxygen exposure through the wood. Chips and spirals give you the wood itself. You can add spirit character separately.

Oak works best in big, dark or strong beers: imperial stouts, barleywines, porters, Scotch ales and strong Belgian ales. In a light lager it tends to dominate.

• American oak. Bold vanilla and coconut. The classic bourbon barrel profile.
  • French oak. Subtler, spicier and finer tannin. Used widely in wine.
  • Hungarian and other European oaks. Somewhere between the two.

Toast level matters as much as origin. Light toast is woody and fresh. Medium toast brings vanilla and caramel. Heavy toast and char lean towards coffee, smoke and burnt sugar. Medium or medium-plus American oak is a sensible first choice for a stout.

Chips have a large surface area for their weight, so they release flavour fast, often within a week or two. Easy to overdo.

Cubes are thicker. They extract more slowly, over weeks to a few months. They give a rounder, more barrel-like result because both the toasted surface and the less toasted interior contribute.

Spirals are long, grooved sticks designed to fit through a carboy neck. They extract at a rate between chips and cubes and are easy to pull out when the beer tastes right.

Avoid oak dust and sawdust. It clouds the beer and is hard to remove.

Starting points for a 20 litre batch:

  • Chips: about 30 to 60 g for one to two weeks.
  • Cubes: about 60 to 90 g for four to eight weeks.
  • Spirals: one or two, for a few weeks, following the maker's guidance.

Taste every few days with a sanitised sampler. Pull the oak as soon as it tastes slightly less oaky than you want, because flavour keeps integrating afterwards. Warm temperatures speed extraction, so in an Indian summer at 28 to 30 °C ambient, check more often than a recipe written for a cold British garage would suggest.

Oak is porous and can hide wild yeast and bacteria. Options include steaming for ten to fifteen minutes, a short boil (which also pulls out some harsh tannin and some flavour) or soaking in a spirit for a week or more. Soaking in whisky or rum adds the spirit character at the same time. Pour off the soaking spirit, or add a measured amount to the beer if you want more of it. Allow for the small ABV change.

Real barrels give beer the spirit that soaked into the staves. With chips or cubes you can get there by soaking the oak in your chosen spirit, or by adding a small, measured dose of spirit at packaging. Start low and taste. A little spirit reads as warmth and depth. A lot reads as a cocktail. Our guide to whisky maturation and casks explains where those barrel flavours come from in the first place.
Oak in a warm Indian flat

Temperature changes everything about oaking. At 30 °C, chips release flavour noticeably faster than at a cool cellar temperature. A strong beer sitting warm for weeks also ages faster in other ways. If you can, oak in a cool spot or in a fermentation fridge set to around 15 to 18 °C, which slows extraction to a pace you can manage.

Buy oak from a homebrew or winemaking supplier, labelled with species and toast. Untreated wood from a timber yard or furniture offcuts may be the wrong species, treated with chemicals or simply never toasted. Raw oak tastes green and harsh.

• Using too much and leaving it too long, giving a harsh, plank-like beer.
  • Oaking a beer that is not finished fermenting. Add oak once fermentation is complete.
  • Splashing during transfers on and off the oak, which oxidises the beer.
  • Reusing the same chips across beers, which carries over flavour and microbes.

Oak is one of several tools for adding depth after fermentation. Knowing when the base beer is right and when the additions are helping it is something you only learn by brewing, tasting and logging every step.
faqs: How long should I leave oak chips in beer?
Usually one to two weeks. Taste every few days and remove them a little before the beer tastes oaky enough.
Which oak is best for a stout?
Medium or medium-plus toast American oak is a good start, giving vanilla, coconut and caramel.
Do I need to sanitise oak chips?
Yes. Steam them, boil briefly or soak in spirit to reduce the risk of wild yeast and bacteria.
It is better not to. They carry flavour and microbes from the last beer and give less each time.
